name: Public Key Encryption Basics
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Math Trick That Runs the Internet
lesson.summary: Public key cryptography lets two strangers who share no secret establish secure communication, resting on classical computing's core asymmetry that some math problems are fast to compute one way and impractically slow to reverse.
lesson.body:
Every time you visit a site whose address starts with https, load your banking app, or send a message through an app advertising end to end encryption, public key cryptography is quietly doing enormous work in the background. It solves a problem that seems almost paradoxical: how can two people who have never met, with no way to safely share a secret in advance, agree on a shared secret over a channel anyone might be listening to? The answer, developed in the 1970s, is one of the more elegant ideas in applied mathematics, resting on classical computing's fundamental asymmetry: computers are extremely fast at some kinds of math and extremely slow at others.

Public key, or asymmetric, cryptography works by giving each participant two related keys instead of one shared secret. A public key can be handed out to literally anyone, published on a website, printed on a business card, it does not need to be kept secret at all. A private key is kept secret by its owner and never shared. The two keys are mathematically linked in a specific way: something encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the matching private key, and a message signed with the private key can be verified by anyone using the matching public key. This lets a stranger encrypt a message that only you can read, and lets you prove a message really came from you, all without either of you ever having exchanged a secret in person.

The trick that makes this work is a mathematical relationship that is easy to compute in one direction and extremely hard to reverse using classical computing methods. The most famous version, RSA, relies on multiplication and factoring: multiplying two large prime numbers together is fast, even for enormous primes hundreds of digits long, but factoring the resulting product back into its two primes is so slow using known classical algorithms that it would take longer than the age of the universe for large enough numbers, even on the fastest supercomputers that exist. Other widely used systems, including Diffie-Hellman key exchange and elliptic curve cryptography, rely on a related but different hard problem, called the discrete logarithm problem, which has the same essential shape: easy to compute forward, extremely hard to reverse.

This easy one way, hard the other way property is not an accident or a side effect. It is the entire security model. Public key cryptography does not claim these problems are mathematically impossible to solve, only that solving them classically requires so much computation that it is impractical within a useful timeframe, even with enormous resources. Nearly every piece of infrastructure built on RSA, Diffie-Hellman, or elliptic curve cryptography, which includes most secure communication on the internet today, from web browsing to banking to messaging to software updates, rests on the assumption that factoring large numbers and computing discrete logarithms will stay computationally impractical.

That assumption is exactly what makes public key cryptography relevant to a book about quantum computing skepticism. Quantum computers are not a general speedup for every computation, but they were shown, in theory, to be specifically and dramatically better at the two problems, factoring and discrete logarithms, that public key cryptography depends on being hard. Understanding that these systems rest on a specific computational assumption, not an unbreakable law, sets up the next chapter's question directly: what happens to that assumption if a sufficiently capable quantum computer gets built.
